name: Trauma-Informed Boundary & Safety Recognition
citation: SAMHSA (2014). SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach. HHS Publication No. (SMA) 14-4884; NIMH (2023). Coping with Traumatic Events.
mechanism: Validating the reality of unpredictable hostility to prevent self-doubt and gaslighting, separating responsibility for another person's actions, and centering physical and emotional safety through personal boundaries and trusted support rather than confrontation.
what_is_controllable: Your own boundaries, emotional distance, physical safety, documenting what happened, and choosing who you reach out to for trusted support.
what_is_not_controllable: The other person's volatile behavior, their anger, whether they act normal afterward, or trying to fix their emotional state.
reframe_template: Their acting normal afterward does not erase what happened earlier. You don't have to convince yourself that the incident was okay just because the atmosphere is calm now. You can acknowledge what happened, recognize the pattern without blaming yourself, and prioritize what keeps you safest and most in control.
action_template: Right now, you don't need to fix their behavior. Give yourself physical or emotional distance, write down what happened while you remember it clearly, and reach out to someone you trust if you need support.
voice_story_template: When someone lashes out and then behaves as though nothing happened, it can leave you questioning your own reaction. But a calm moment afterward does not erase what happened before it. You don't have to take responsibility for another person's behavior. Focus instead on what you can control: your own boundaries, your safety, and reaching out to someone you trust when you need support.
safety_rule: Do not encourage confrontation or direct argument with a volatile person. Emphasize physical and emotional safety, trusted external support, and clear boundaries.

character.description: a young adult navigating a tense home environment
character.appearance: short dark hair, guarded but resilient posture, attentive eyes

scenes.title: 2. REFRAMING
scenes.visual: standing by a doorway taking a calm grounding breath, looking with steady clarity, recognizing the pattern without self-blame
scenes.dialogue: His acting normal doesn't erase what happened. I can recognize the pattern without blaming myself for it.
scenes.caption: You don't have to rewrite what happened simply because the situation became calm.

scenes.title: 3. RESOLUTION
scenes.visual: sitting in a quiet safe private room holding a phone to message a trusted friend, holding a personal journal, calm and grounded
scenes.dialogue: I can't control his reaction. I can choose what I do next and who I turn to for support.
scenes.caption: Focus on safety, support, and the parts of the situation you can control.

name: Decatastrophizing & Controllable Preparation
citation: Beck, A. T., Emery, G., & Greenberg, R. L. (1985). Anxiety Disorders and Phobias: A Cognitive Perspective. Basic Books; APA (2020). Coping with Performance and Evaluative Stress.
mechanism: Separating catastrophic predictions from genuine probabilities, recognizing that anxiety is an anticipated reaction rather than a guarantee of failure, and redirecting cognitive energy to tangible preparation steps.
what_is_controllable: Your preparation, how you organize your review or interview talking points, taking rest breaks, and your physical breathing.
what_is_not_controllable: The exact questions you will be asked, the evaluator's moods or preconceptions, or predicting the future with certainty.
reframe_template: Feeling nervous is a natural physical response to something that matters to you, not evidence that failure is guaranteed. You don't know the exact outcome yet; you can prepare for the specific parts you directly control.
action_template: Choose one concrete preparation task right in front of you—such as reviewing one key topic or rehearsing one response—and complete it before pausing for a break.
voice_story_template: When an important evaluation is approaching, fear often convinces us that failure is already decided. But feeling anxious does not mean you are going to fail; it simply means this matters to you. You cannot predict the exact outcome today, but you can prepare the pieces within your control. Focus on taking one structured step forward right now.
safety_rule: Encourage realistic expectations and adequate sleep rather than unhealthy all-night cramming or panic-driven avoidance.

character.description: a focused young adult preparing for an evaluation
character.appearance: short dark hair, expressive focused eyes, earnest posture
character.clothing: wearing a navy blue knit sweater and dark trousers

scenes.title: 1. PROBLEM
scenes.visual: sitting at a desk with an interview schedule and notes, hands gripping head in anxiety, dim room with harsh screen glow

scenes.title: 2. REFRAMING
scenes.visual: sitting back slightly in chair, taking a slow deliberate breath, looking objectively at structured notes with steady focus
scenes.dialogue: Being nervous means this matters to me, not that failure is guaranteed. I'll focus on what I can prepare.
scenes.caption: Anxiety is an emotional signal, not a forecast of what is certain to happen.

scenes.title: 3. RESOLUTION
scenes.visual: sitting upright at an organized desk, reviewing three key points on a notepad with calm confidence, warm daylight
scenes.dialogue: I'll practice my main talking points once, then give my mind time to rest.
scenes.caption: Channel nervous energy into one manageable piece of preparation.

name: Checking Assumptions & De-escalating Mind-Reading
citation: Linehan, M. M. (1993). Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment of Borderline Personality Disorder. Guilford Press; APA (2018). Interpersonal Effectiveness & Social Anxiety.
mechanism: Differentiating between observable facts (e.g., someone hasn't replied yet) and internal interpretations (e.g., 'they hate me'). Prevents social withdrawal and catastrophic assumptions regarding interpersonal connection.
what_is_controllable: Your own time, activities, how you care for yourself right now, and communicating directly if appropriate later.
what_is_not_controllable: Another person's immediate availability, their schedule, work pressures, or how quickly they check their phone.
reframe_template: An unanswered message or silence is an absence of information, not proof of rejection. People are often busy, preoccupied, or overwhelmed by their own day. You don't have to fill the silence with the worst possible assumption.
action_template: Step away from the screen, engage in an engaging offline task or talk to another supportive contact, and give the situation time to breathe without jumping to conclusions.
voice_story_template: When someone doesn't reply or seems distant, it's easy for our minds to fill in the blank with rejection. But silence is simply a pause, not proof that someone dislikes you. You cannot control when other people reply, but you can control what you do with your time. Step back, breathe, and focus on your own afternoon.
safety_rule: Avoid advising passive-aggressive texting or frantic double-messaging. Encourage patience and healthy social grounding.

scenes.title: 2. REFRAMING

scenes.title: 3. RESOLUTION
scenes.visual: standing up in a sunlit kitchen making a cup of tea, looking relaxed and focused on personal interests
scenes.dialogue: I'll let them respond in their own time and focus on enjoying my own evening.
scenes.caption: Give relationships room to breathe while attending to your own present wellbeing.

name: Cognitive Defusion & Regret Release
citation: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (1999). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: An Experiential Approach to Behavior Change. Guilford Press; Nolen-Hoeksema, S. (2000). The role of rumination in depressive disorders.
mechanism: Recognizing that mentally replaying a past moment cannot alter it. Stepping back to observe repetitive thoughts as passing mental events rather than urgent commands to analyze, freeing attention for present constructive action.
what_is_controllable: Where you direct your attention right now, self-kindness toward past human mistakes, and choices in the present moment.
what_is_not_controllable: The event that already happened yesterday, the words already said, or erasing past discomfort instantly.
reframe_template: Replaying the past over and over feels like solving a problem, but it is actually just keeping the discomfort alive. What happened occurred in the past; you cannot edit yesterday, but you can choose what receives your attention right now.
action_template: Name the thought gently ('I notice I am replaying yesterday'), take three physical grounding breaths, and engage your senses in an immediate sensory activity.
voice_story_template: When a past mistake or awkward moment replays in your head, it can feel like you need to solve it again. But replaying the memory cannot change what happened; it only drains your energy in the present. Acknowledge that you are human, let the thought pass without fighting it, and bring your focus gently back to where your feet are right now.
safety_rule: Ground in the immediate present environment if rumination escalates into intense shame.

scenes.caption: Replaying the past can feel like problem-solving, but it often just traps us in regret.

scenes.title: 2. REFRAMING
scenes.visual: standing by an open window, feeling a gentle breeze, placing a hand on chest with self-compassion
scenes.dialogue: Replaying it won't change yesterday. I can allow myself to be human and learn without punishment.
scenes.caption: You cannot rewrite yesterday, but you can choose not to punish yourself in the present.

scenes.title: 3. RESOLUTION
scenes.visual: sitting at a clean wooden table drinking a glass of cool water, sketching or journaling calmly in bright light
scenes.dialogue: I'm letting that moment go. I'm focusing on what's right here in front of me.
scenes.caption: Gently redirect your attention to what is real and actionable right now.

name: Self-Compassionate Restructuring
citation: Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity; Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression.
mechanism: Separating a single setback or mistake from one's entire identity and worth. Replacing punitive internal criticism with constructive, balanced accountability and kindness.
what_is_controllable: The specific task to correct or learn from, your self-talk, and asking for clarification or help.
what_is_not_controllable: Expecting yourself to never make an error, or having flawless performance at all times.
reframe_template: Making a mistake or encountering a setback is an isolated event, not a permanent definition of who you are. Struggling with a challenge does not make you useless or incapable; it means you are learning something difficult.
action_template: Speak to yourself with the same constructive patience you would offer a trusted friend, and identify one small corrective step rather than attacking your character.
voice_story_template: When you make a mistake, self-criticism can quickly escalate into harsh labels like being a failure or useless. But a single setback does not define your worth or capability. Mistakes are part of being human. Treat yourself with the same patience you would give someone you care about, and take one constructive step forward.
safety_rule: If harsh self-labeling borders on active hopelessness or self-harm, screen immediately for crisis support.

scenes.dialogue: I'll fix this one specific error patiently, step by step.
scenes.caption: Respond to setbacks with constructive adjustment rather than harsh self-punishment.

name: Locus of Control & Grounding in Uncertainty
citation: Rotter, J. B. (1966). Generalized expectancies for internal versus external control. Psychological Monographs; APA (2021). Managing Uncertainty in Stressful Times.
mechanism: Mapping ambiguous stressors into what is truly within personal agency versus what is uncontrollable. Grounding physiological arousal in the present to reduce threat vigilance.
what_is_controllable: Your current physical safety, your daily routine, how you spend the next hour, and asking for factual information.
what_is_not_controllable: How the unpredictable future unfolds, circumstances outside your agency, or other people's decisions.
reframe_template: Not knowing what will happen is deeply uncomfortable, but uncertainty does not automatically mean catastrophe. You do not need to figure out the next five years today; you only need to navigate the hour in front of you.
action_template: Anchor your feet firmly on the ground, take a steady breath, and complete one simple routine action—like drinking water or tidying your immediate space.
voice_story_template: When the future feels ambiguous, our minds naturally search for threats, making uncertainty feel dangerous. But not knowing what lies ahead does not mean something bad is bound to happen. You don't have to carry the whole future today. Ground yourself in what is real and safe right now, and take this one hour at a time.
safety_rule: Focus on immediate predictability and steady routines when uncertainty causes acute distress.

scenes.title: 2. REFRAMING

scenes.title: 3. RESOLUTION
scenes.visual: sitting at a tidy kitchen table writing down two manageable tasks for today, bright clear daylight
scenes.dialogue: I will focus on the small routine tasks I can control today and take it one hour at a time.
scenes.caption: Anchor your agency in the present rather than wrestling with the unknown.

name: Compassionate Grief Processing & Attachment Support
citation: Bowlby, J. (1980). Loss: Sadness and Depression; APA (2019). Grieving Relationships & Emotional Distress.
mechanism: Validating the genuine pain of disconnection as a natural attachment response rather than personal deficiency. Encouraging self-soothing, steady routines, and connection with safe friends rather than isolation.
what_is_controllable: Allowing yourself space to feel sad without self-blame, maintaining sleep and meals, and turning to trusted friends or family.
what_is_not_controllable: The other person's decisions, undoing the past, or rushing the natural timeline of emotional recovery.
reframe_template: The grief you feel is proof of your capacity to care, not evidence that you are unlovable or broken. Healing from loss takes time and comes in waves; you do not have to force yourself to 'just get over it' today.
action_template: Wrap yourself in something warm, allow yourself to rest without judgment, and reach out to one safe person just to share presence without having to perform.
voice_story_template: Going through a breakup or deep loss shakes your sense of safety and routine. It makes complete sense that you can't stop thinking about it—grief is love with nowhere to go. You don't have to pretend everything is fine today. Be gentle with your heart, take care of your basic needs, and let a trusted friend stand by your side.
safety_rule: Validate emotional sorrow without encouraging intrusive contact or stalking behaviors.

name: Micro-Action & Overwhelm Reduction
citation: D'Zurilla, T. J., & Nezu, A. M. (2007). Problem-Solving Therapy. Springer; APA (2020). Coping with Stress & Cognitive Overload.
mechanism: Interrupting analysis paralysis caused by looking at an entire mountain of tasks. Shrinking focus strictly down to a single 5-minute micro-action to bypass cognitive overload and rebuild momentum.
what_is_controllable: Choosing just ONE tiny physical action right now, setting a 5-minute timer, and giving yourself permission to ignore the rest for twenty minutes.
what_is_not_controllable: Finishing all twenty obligations in a single afternoon, or instantly eliminating all project demands at once.
reframe_template: You do not have to conquer all twenty tasks simultaneously. You only need to touch one small corner of one task. Momentum does not come before starting; starting one tiny action is what creates momentum.
action_template: Pick the simplest sub-task on your list—something that takes under 5 minutes. Put everything else out of sight, set a timer, and do just that one thing.
voice_story_template: When your to-do list feels endless, your brain treats it like an impossible wall, leaving you paralyzed. But you don't have to complete twenty things right now. You only need to take one micro-step. Pick the smallest, easiest piece, set aside the rest for a moment, and let one simple action get you moving again.
safety_rule: Avoid setting large, perfectionistic multi-hour study goals when the person is actively frozen.

scenes.title: 2. REFRAMING

scenes.title: 3. RESOLUTION

scenes.dialogue: I'll spend five minutes on this one step, and celebrate making a start.
scenes.caption: One small step forward is enough to break the freeze and start momentum.

name: Values Clarification & Comparison Defusion
citation: Hayes, S. C. et al. (1999). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy; Festinger, L. (1954). A theory of social comparison processes.
mechanism: Recognizing that social comparisons juxtapose one's internal messy reality against another person's curated external highlight reel. Re-anchoring focus to personal, intrinsic values rather than external status metrics.
what_is_controllable: Your own values, your personal definitions of meaningful progress, and muting triggers that provoke comparison.
what_is_not_controllable: What other people choose to showcase, their timelines, advantages, or achievements.
reframe_template: You are comparing your behind-the-scenes struggles to everyone else's public highlight reel. Another person's success does not diminish your worth or speed. Your journey has its own unique context, pacing, and value.
action_template: Put down social media, write down two things that genuinely matter to you independent of anyone else's approval, and honor your own pace today.
voice_story_template: When you look around and feel like everyone is achieving more or moving faster, it is easy to feel inadequate. But you are comparing your daily reality to other people's curated highlights. Life is not a race against others. Step back from the comparisons, honor your own timeline, and focus on the personal values that matter to you.
safety_rule: Emphasize intrinsic values rather than competing harder to prove superiority.

scenes.caption: Anchor your sense of worth in what is true and meaningful to your own life.

name: Physiological Down-Regulation & Rest Permission
citation: APA (2022). Stress and Recovery in Burnout; Porges, S. W. (2011). The Polyvagal Theory.
mechanism: Validating physical exhaustion as biological feedback that nervous system resources are depleted, rather than moral failure or lack of discipline. Giving unreserved permission for restorative downtime.
what_is_controllable: Allowing yourself to stop pushing, taking a horizontal rest, drinking water, and scheduling restorative sleep.
what_is_not_controllable: Forcing your nervous system to operate on empty reserves through sheer willpower.
reframe_template: Your exhaustion is not laziness or weakness; it is your body's vital physiological signal that your battery is empty. Rest is not a reward you have to earn after collapsing; it is the biological prerequisite for functioning at all.
action_template: Close your eyes, lower your shoulders away from your ears, and give yourself full, unapologetic permission to rest for 30 minutes without guilt.
voice_story_template: When you are completely burnt out, trying to force productivity only increases your distress. Your tiredness is not a flaw in your willpower; it is your body telling you that you have given everything you had. Listen to that signal. Giving yourself permission to rest is not quitting—it is how your nervous system heals and restores.
safety_rule: Ensure the user prioritizes physical safety, hydration, and sleep.

scenes.dialogue: I'm turning off the pressure and allowing my body to recharge peacefully.
scenes.caption: Allow your nervous system to down-regulate and recover without guilt.

name: Grounded Perspective & Balanced Action
citation: APA (2020). Evidence-Based Stress Management; Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy.
mechanism: Validating the emotional weight of a difficult moment, checking whether thoughts are assuming worst-case scenarios, and identifying one realistic constructive action within personal agency.
what_is_controllable: Your response today, taking care of yourself, and one constructive next action.
what_is_not_controllable: Past events or fixing everything all at once.
reframe_template: Having doubts or feeling unsettled is a normal human experience. You do not have to have everything figured out right now; you can take one small step and let the rest unfold in time.
action_template: Take a deep breath, write down the one single thing that would help you feel most steady right now, and take care of it with kindness.
voice_story_template: When a situation feels heavy or confusing, it is easy to feel weighed down by self-doubt. But you do not have to solve your entire life today. Take a pause, acknowledge how you feel, and remember that you only need to take one small constructive step right now.
safety_rule: Keep recommendations manageable, grounded, and empathetic.
